We're looking for stories where creativity meets technology in small-town contexts, and where local artists and storytellers are finding new ways to reach audiences beyond geography.
_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling' — how communities create, preserve, and share culture, with particular interest in the Cariboo and rural BC.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-14: medical and health research with no cultural angle; resource-economy stories with no cultural framing; wildlife and nature stories without a creative or community-media context; data centre and AI investment news; geopolitical conflict, war, and crime coverage; financial market stories.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. A Cariboo tie raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band: judge on the strength of the arts/culture/storytelling reporting first.
- 80-100: Excellent arts, culture, or storytelling journalism. Cariboo/Williams Lake arts news lands here (arts council grants, murals, local festivals, Indigenous film, community theatre, heritage programs, a Cariboo author or artist honoured) — and so does outstanding national or international cultural reporting with real depth.
- 55-79: Solid arts/culture/media journalism. Rural BC and Canadian cultural coverage, CBC Arts features, regional festivals, community media projects, heritage preservation, creative-economy stories, digital storytelling tools and platforms, community media tech (podcasting, streaming, local publishing), animation and film production. Most genuine cultural journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Mainstream entertainment-industry coverage with modest substance (awards-show results, film/TV/music business news, publishing trade news).
- 15-29: Tangentially creative — a tech feature touching media/publishing/streaming, or Cariboo civic news with no arts angle.

ANCHORS: 'Repatriated Tŝilhqot'in baskets arrive in Williams Lake from Brooklyn Museum' → 95. 'How a BC First Nation is digitizing its oral histories' → 80. 'CBC Arts: the quiet revival of small-town prairie theatre' → 68. 'Netflix reports Q3 subscriber growth' → 20.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] ‘I do not know if the doctor survived’: young mothers recall ‘living hell’ of Nepal’s floods
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Kalpana Nepali was seven months pregnant when the flash floods hit last month, while Pooja Pariyal spent three days on a hospital roof waiting to be rescued. Now, they are living precariously in temporary shelters

For three days, Pooja Pariyal waited on the roof of Trishuli hospital with her three-month-old daughter, Ridhika. On the ground below and around the building, most of her town had been destroyed and churned into a sea of mud in the catastrophic flash floods that surged through the Himayalan border region of Nepal and Tibet in August.

“Those three days were living hell for me, with no food, no working toilet and no one to help with the baby,” she says. “I had nothing to clean my baby’s soiled clothes. My milk supply had reduced because I was hungry and this poor little thing would cry her lungs out.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Black hole jets may decide the fate of entire galaxies
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Powerful jets from supermassive black holes can disturb star-forming gas far beyond a galaxy’s visible edge, leaving a glowing trail hundreds of thousands of light-years long. By keeping this gas hot and preventing it from falling inward, the jets may help determine whether a galaxy keeps forming stars or becomes quiet.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] One green shoot at a time: the women restoring mangrove forests in the oil-ravaged Niger delta
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

In a region of Nigeria blighted by decades of pollution, Martha Agbani and her team are not just replanting trees but regaining ownership of their lost lands and livelihoods

A toxic landscape was familiar to Martha Agbani when she was growing up – the smell of crude oil in the air, rivers running black and trees dying on the banks. In Ogoniland, in Nigeria’s oil-exploited Niger delta, Agbani saw the spills rot away the mangrove forests and destroy the livelihoods of communities around her.

Now, she is training women to plant them back – one fragile green shoot at a time.

items.title: [npr.org] El Niño fuels Pacific storms as Atlantic lacks hurricanes
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

An exceptionally strong El Niño is driving sharply different hurricane seasons in the Pacific and Atlantic. By Sept. 25, the Pacific had recorded 41 named storms, including 18 hurricanes, while the Atlantic had produced no hurricanes [npr.org#1]. Scientists cited El Niño as a key reason for the contrast [npr.org#1][abcnews.com#1]. Hurricane Polo rapidly intensified off Mexico, while Hurricane Nolo strengthened south of Hawaii. Nolo threatened the Big Island with extreme rain, flash flooding and mudslides. Forecasts called for 15 to 30 inches of rain in parts of the Big Island, with higher local totals possible; Nolo was not expected to make landfall [nasa.gov#1][earthsky.org#1][gpb.org#1][koaa.com#1].
